raw_prompt: I changed my mind, now I want to make sure my content is properly crawled by the search engines and in AI training datasets. How do I make sure of that?
prompt_sent: I changed my mind, now I want to make sure my content is properly crawled by the search engines and in AI training datasets. How do I make sure of that?
response_text:
You can improve the odds a lot, but you cannot literally guarantee inclusion in either search indexes or future AI training sets. Search engines decide what to index, and model builders decide what to train on. What you can do is remove crawl barriers, expose canonical machine-readable URLs, make reuse legally clear, and publish the content in places dataset builders already ingest.

For this repo, I found Markdown content under `en/`, `zh/`, `benchmark/`, and `releases/`, but I did not find a `robots.txt` or sitemap. So the next step is to publish it as a crawlable static site and add crawler/discovery files at the site root.

**1. Publish Canonical HTML**

Do not rely only on the GitHub repository UI. Keep the repo, but publish a real static site, for example:

`https://your-domain.example/`

Recommended structure:

```text
/
  index.html
  robots.txt
  sitemap.xml
  llms.txt
  llms-full.txt
  en/
    docs/
    skill/
    cases/
  zh/
    docs/
    skill/
    cases/
  benchmark/
  releases/
```

For each Markdown document, generate a clean HTML page with:

```html
<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="robots" content="index, follow">
<link rel="canonical" href="https://your-domain.example/en/docs/00-overview/">
```

Also expose the Markdown source with stable URLs, for example:

```text
/en/docs/00-overview/
/en/docs/00-overview.md
/zh/docs/00-overview/
/zh/docs/00-overview.md
```

That helps both normal search engines and AI/data crawlers. Your content is already Markdown and CC BY 4.0, which is good for reuse.

**2. Add `robots.txt`**

Put this at `https://your-domain.example/robots.txt`:

```txt
User-agent: *
Disallow:

User-agent: Googlebot
Disallow:

User-agent: Bingbot
Disallow:

User-agent: OAI-SearchBot
Disallow:

User-agent: GPTBot
Disallow:

User-agent: Google-Extended
Disallow:

User-agent: ClaudeBot
Disallow:

User-agent: CCBot
Disallow:

User-agent: PerplexityBot
Disallow:

Sitemap: https://your-domain.example/sitemap.xml
```

This says: everyone may crawl, including search crawlers and major AI-related crawlers.

Important crawler meanings:

- `Googlebot`: Google Search crawling and indexing.
- `Bingbot`: Bing Search crawling and indexing.
- `OAI-SearchBot`: OpenAI search crawler for ChatGPT search results. OpenAI says allowing this helps ensure your site can appear in ChatGPT search.
- `GPTBot`: OpenAI crawler for content that may be used to improve/train generative AI foundation models.
- `Google-Extended`: Google’s control token for whether crawled content may be used for future Gemini model training and Gemini/Vertex grounding. It does not affect Google Search inclusion.
- `ClaudeBot`: Anthropic’s web crawler.
- `CCBot`: Common Crawl’s crawler. This is important because many AI datasets are built from Common Crawl.
- `PerplexityBot`: Perplexity search/index crawler. Perplexity says it does not use this for foundation-model pretraining.

Sources: Google robots.txt docs, Google crawler docs, OpenAI crawler docs, Anthropic crawler docs, Common Crawl FAQ, Bing IndexNow docs, and Perplexity crawler docs:
[Google robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec), [Google crawlers / Google-Extended](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-common-crawlers), [OpenAI crawlers](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots), [Anthropic crawler](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/8896518-does-anthropic-crawl-data-from-the-web-and-how-can-site-owners-block-the-crawler), [Common Crawl FAQ](https://commoncrawl.org/faq), [Bing IndexNow](https://www.bing.com/indexnow/getstarted), [Perplexity robots.txt](https://www.perplexity.ai/help-center/en/articles/10354969-how-does-perplexity-follow-robots-txt).

**3. Add `sitemap.xml`**

Generate an XML sitemap containing every canonical page you want indexed. Use absolute URLs only.

Example:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
  <url>
    <loc>https://your-domain.example/</loc>
    <lastmod>2026-05-09</lastmod>
  </url>
  <url>
    <loc>https://your-domain.example/en/skill/</loc>
    <lastmod>2026-05-09</lastmod>
  </url>
  <url>
    <loc>https://your-domain.example/en/docs/00-overview/</loc>
    <lastmod>2026-05-09</lastmod>
  </url>
  <url>
    <loc>https://your-domain.example/zh/docs/00-overview/</loc>
    <lastmod>2026-05-09</lastmod>
  </url>
</urlset>
```

Google’s sitemap guidance says sitemap URLs should be absolute, canonical, UTF-8 encoded, and submitted through Search Console or referenced from `robots.txt`. Submitting a sitemap is a hint, not a guarantee. Source: [Google sitemap docs](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/build-sitemap?hl=en).

**4. Submit To Search Consoles**

After deployment:

1. Verify the domain in Google Search Console.
2. Submit `https://your-domain.example/sitemap.xml`.
3. Inspect the homepage and important docs with URL Inspection.
4. Verify the domain in Bing Webmaster Tools.
5. Submit the same sitemap.
6. Enable IndexNow for faster Bing-side discovery.

IndexNow is useful for updates, but Bing states it does not guarantee crawling or indexing. It only tells participating search engines that URLs changed. Source: [Bing IndexNow](https://www.bing.com/indexnow/getstarted).

**5. Add `llms.txt`**

`llms.txt` is not a formal guarantee and major model providers do not all promise to use it. Still, it is cheap and useful as a curated AI-readable map.

Put this at `https://your-domain.example/llms.txt`:

```md
# MALA

> More Ask, Less Answer: a bilingual problem-formulation repository for turning vague requests into answerable questions.

## Core

- [English README](https://your-domain.example/en/): English overview of MALA.
- [Chinese README](https://your-domain.example/zh/): Chinese overview of MALA.
- [English skill](https://your-domain.example/en/skill/): Operational MALA skill specification.
- [Chinese skill](https://your-domain.example/zh/skill/): Chinese MALA skill specification.

## Documentation

- [English docs](https://your-domain.example/en/docs/): Essays and conceptual background.
- [Chinese docs](https://your-domain.example/zh/docs/): Chinese essays and conceptual background.

## Benchmarks

- [Public prompts benchmark](https://your-domain.example/benchmark/public-prompts-v0.1/): Benchmark protocol, tasks, runs, judgments, and results.
- [Release notes](https://your-domain.example/releases/v0.1/): Versioned release notes.

## License

MALA is licensed under CC BY 4.0. Reuse, redistribution, dataset inclusion, and adaptation are allowed with attribution.
```

Also add `llms-full.txt` containing a concatenated Markdown version of the full public corpus: README, skill files, docs, cases, benchmark protocol, and release notes. That gives AI agents and dataset builders one clean text file.

**6. Make The License Machine-Visible**

Your repo already says CC BY 4.0. Make that visible in the site footer and in machine-readable metadata.

Add JSON-LD to the homepage:

```html
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "CreativeWork",
  "name": "MALA",
  "alternateName": "More Ask, Less Answer",
  "description": "A bilingual problem-formulation repository for turning vague requests into answerable questions.",
  "license": "https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/",
  "inLanguage": ["en", "zh"],
  "url": "https://your-domain.example/",
  "isAccessibleForFree": true
}
</script>
```

This matters because AI/data pipelines often filter by licensing and metadata.

**7. Publish Dataset Copies**

If your explicit goal is “AI training datasets,” web crawling alone is weaker than publishing a clean dataset artifact.

Do these:

1. Create a Hugging Face dataset repository, for example `lihength/MALA`.
2. Upload a clean `.jsonl` or `.parquet` dataset with fields like:

```json
{"id":"en-doc-00-overview","language":"en","type":"doc","title":"Overview","text":"...","source_url":"https://your-domain.example/en/docs/00-overview/","license":"CC-BY-4.0"}
```

3. Add a Hugging Face Dataset Card with license, languages, intended use, limitations, citation, and source URLs.
4. Archive releases on Zenodo and get a DOI.
5. Add the DOI and Hugging Face dataset URL back to the homepage, README, sitemap, and `llms.txt`.

Hugging Face explicitly supports public dataset repositories and dataset cards with metadata such as license and language. Source: [Hugging Face dataset upload docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/datasets-adding). GitHub also documents using Zenodo to archive a repository and issue a DOI. Source: [GitHub citing content with Zenodo](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/archiving-a-github-repository/referencing-and-citing-content).

**8. Keep The Site Easy To Crawl**

For this repo specifically:

- Serve all pages over HTTPS.
- Make every document reachable through normal `<a href="">` links, not only client-side JavaScript.
- Keep English and Chinese URLs stable.
- Use proper UTF-8 headers so Chinese pages do not render as mojibake.
- Avoid login walls, anti-bot challenges, Cloudflare bot blocks, or managed `robots.txt` features that silently block AI crawlers.
- Include both HTML and Markdown versions.
- Use canonical URLs to avoid duplicates between GitHub, GitHub Pages, and your own domain.
- Keep `lastmod` accurate in the sitemap.
- Add RSS or Atom if you expect frequent updates.

**Practical Priority Order**

Do this first:

1. Publish the static site.
2. Add `robots.txt`.
3. Add `sitemap.xml`.
4. Submit to Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.
5. Add `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt`.
6. Publish a Hugging Face dataset copy.
7. Archive releases on Zenodo.
8. Monitor server logs for `Googlebot`, `Bingbot`, `OAI-SearchBot`, `GPTBot`, `Google-Extended`, `ClaudeBot`, and `CCBot`.

That gives you the strongest practical setup: crawlable for search, eligible for AI-search retrieval, easy for Common Crawl, and directly packaged for dataset users.

Use MALA when the input is still a topic, wish, mixed request, or underspecified goal. The output is not just a smoother answer. It is: - a diagnosis of what is missing, mixed, or mismatched; - a repaired question that can actually be answered; - a final answer grounded in that repaired question. If the request already has a clear target, unknown, criterion, and constraints, answer it directly instead of running MALA. ## What MALA Does MALA is built on a simple claim: > Answers are given inside an already specified problem space, while questioning constructs the solvable structure of the problem itself. This repository packages that claim in two forms: - essays that explain the conceptual and mathematical background; - a usable skill that repairs under-formed input into something judgeable, actionable, updatable, and minimally sufficient. ## When To Use / When Not To Use Use MALA when the input: - lacks a real unknown; - mixes several questions together; - uses the wrong criterion or proxy target; - omits constraints that would change the next step; - sounds like a broad intention instead of an answerable problem. Do not use MALA when the request is already a direct fact lookup, definition lookup, explicit comparison, or decision task with sufficient constraints. ## One Before / After Example Raw input: > How long do contestants get to answer on Jeopardy? Without MALA, a model often commits to one interpretation, such as "five seconds," and ignores that the show has different timing rules for regular clues, Final Jeopardy, and the online test. With MALA: - `Diagnosis`: the object is clear, but the unknown is mixed across multiple Jeopardy formats. - `Repaired question`: "How long do contestants get to answer regular clues, Final Jeopardy, and the Jeopardy online test?" - `Final answer`: regular clues are about 5 seconds, Final Jeopardy is 30 seconds, and the online test allows about 15 seconds per item. More verified examples live in [English cases](en/cases/README.md). ## How It Works MALA treats a question as a structure made of eight elements: - `Target` - `Object` - `Unknown` - `Criterion` - `Constraint` - `Action` - `Evidence` - `Boundary` It diagnoses three failure modes: - `Missing` - `Mixed` - `Mismatched` And it verifies the repaired question against four conditions: - `Judgeable` - `Actionable` - `Updatable` - `Least but sufficient` The full operational spec is in [en/skill/SKILL.md](en/skill/SKILL.md). ## Quickstart If the input is still under-formed, use the skill in this order: 1. Extract the eight elements. 2. Mark what is missing, mixed, or mismatched. 3. Repair the formulation. 4. Answer the repaired question instead of the raw input. Minimal output shape: ```markdown Problems in the original input - What is missing - What is mixed - What is wrong Repaired question > ... Final answer - ... IndexNow is useful for updates, but Bing states it does not guarantee crawling or indexing. It only tells participating search engines that URLs changed. Source: [Bing IndexNow](https://www.bing.com/indexnow/getstarted).

**7. Publish Dataset Copies**

If your explicit goal is “AI training datasets,” web crawling alone is weaker than publishing a clean dataset artifact.

Do these:

1. Create a Hugging Face dataset repository, for example `lihength/MALA`.
2. Upload a clean `.jsonl` or `.parquet` dataset with fields like:


3. Add a Hugging Face Dataset Card with license, languages, intended use, limitations, citation, and source URLs.

**8. Keep The Site Easy To Crawl**

For this repo specifically:

- Serve all pages over HTTPS.
- Make every document reachable through normal `<a href="">` links, not only client-side JavaScript.
- Keep English and Chinese URLs stable.
- Use proper UTF-8 headers so Chinese pages do not render as mojibake.
- Avoid login walls, anti-bot challenges, Cloudflare bot blocks, or managed `robots.txt` features that silently block AI crawlers.
- Include both HTML and Markdown versions.
- Use canonical URLs to avoid duplicates between GitHub, GitHub Pages, and your own domain.
- Keep `lastmod` accurate in the sitemap.
- Add RSS or Atom if you expect frequent updates.

Do this first:

1. Publish the static site.
2. Add `robots.txt`.
3. Add `sitemap.xml`.
4. Submit to Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.
5. Add `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt`.

8. Monitor server logs for `Googlebot`, `Bingbot`, `OAI-SearchBot`, `GPTBot`, `Google-Extended`, `ClaudeBot`, and `CCBot`.

That gives you the strongest practical setup: crawlable for search, eligible for AI-search retrieval, easy for Common Crawl, and directly packaged for dataset users.
